name: Jardins do Palácio de Cristal
short: A 19th-century romantic park around the site of the Crystal Palace (1865–1951), with views over the Douro and the Atlantic.
long: The Crystal Palace Gardens are a romantic park in the Massarelos area, laid out in the 1860s around the Crystal Palace. The 1865 palace, modelled on London's Crystal Palace, was demolished in 1951 and replaced by the Rosa Mota Pavilion. From the park's terraces and avenues there are panoramic views over the Douro, the Atlantic and the city. It is now one of Porto's favourite places for a stroll.
history:
The Crystal Palace was built to a design by the English architect Thomas Dillen Jones in granite, iron and glass, modelled on London's Crystal Palace. Construction began in 1861, and on 18 September 1865 the palace was inaugurated by King Luís I.

The palace was built for the Porto International Exhibition, which drew 3,139 exhibitors from Portugal and many countries in Europe and beyond. In 1865 the first public Christmas tree in Portugal was put up here.

The park around the palace was laid out in the 1860s by the German landscape architect Émile David. The gardens retain avenues of lime and chestnut trees, camellias, ginkgos, araucarias and a rose garden; they cover about 9.57 hectares.

In 1933 the palace and gardens were bought by Porto City Council. During its 86 years the palace hosted a rose exhibition (1879), the first fine-arts bazaar exhibition (1881) and the Portuguese Colonial Exhibition (1934).

In 1951 the palace was demolished to make way for the Sports Pavilion (today's Pavilhão Rosa Mota, also known as Super Bock Arena), designed by the architect José Carlos Loureiro. Public protest kept the name Crystal Palace alive for the gardens.
facts: The Crystal Palace (1865) was designed by Thomas Dillen Jones, modelled on London's Crystal Palace.
The palace measured 150 metres long by 72 wide, with three naves, in granite, iron and glass.
It was inaugurated on 18 September 1865 by King Luís I for the Porto International Exhibition, with 3,139 exhibitors.
In 1865 it hosted the first public Christmas tree in Portugal.
The gardens were laid out from the 1860s by the German landscape architect Émile David and cover about 9.57 hectares.
The palace was demolished in 1951; the pavilion now on the site is the Pavilhão Rosa Mota (Super Bock Arena).
Its avenues and viewpoints offer panoramas over the Douro, the Atlantic and the city.
tip: Come at sunset: the viewpoint by the Avenida das Tílias has the finest view over the Douro. Entry to the gardens is free, and the Museu Romântico and Solar do Vinho do Porto are nearby.
